result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.count_multi_edges()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Count multi-edges (parallel edges between same node pair). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L9590-L9664){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.count_multi_edges() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Count multi-edges](/assets/graphs/count-multi-edges.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Four nodes in a row with two parallel edges between A and B, three between B and C, and one between C and D. For each pair the first edge is ink and the extras are in the accent color; the card counts the extras: 1 + 2 = 3." width="100%"} Groups edges by their (source, target) pair and counts the edges beyond the first one in each group. For example, if there are 3 edges from `A` to `B`, this counts 2 of them. In other words, the result is how many edges you would remove to leave at most one edge per pair, and `count_edges() - count_multi_edges()` is the number of distinct pairs. Repeated self-loops on the same node are counted the same way. Multi-edges are legitimate in many models (multiple flights between two cities, repeated transactions between two accounts, several co-authored papers), but they can also be unintended duplicates from data loading. Use this count to: - measure how much repetition a multigraph contains - detect accidental duplicate edges after an import - decide whether to collapse duplicates (e.g. with `simplify()`) before running algorithms that assume a simple graph Pairs are matched by the source and target as stored, so in a directed graph `A->B` and `B->A` are different pairs. The same matching is used for undirected graphs, which means an edge added as `B--A` is not paired with one added as `A--B` here (whereas `is_simple()` treats them as parallel). The count covers the whole graph and ignores the current selection. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of duplicate edges (beyond first edge per pair). `0` if no pair has more than one edge. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Only edges beyond the first between a given pair count as "multi" -- here two of the three parallel `A->B` edges are extras, while the reverse `B->A` edge is a separate pair and isn't counted at all: ::: {#e6d81b5f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "B"), # multi-edge ("A", "B"), # another multi-edge ("B", "A"), # different direction, not a duplicate ] ) ) graph.count_multi_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: A route network with repeated flights shows how the count relates to the number of distinct routes: five flights over three routes means two extra flights: ::: {#90e63502 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["NYC", "LAX", "SFO"]) .add_edges( [("NYC", "LAX"), ("NYC", "LAX"), ("NYC", "LAX"), ("LAX", "SFO"), ("SFO", "NYC")] ) ) extras = flights.count_multi_edges() extras, flights.count_edges() - extras ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (2, 3) ``` ::: :::
